paragraphs: An actor-critic learner uses estimated values to guide improvements to its policy. If those estimates are too optimistic, policy learning can follow misleading signals. This paper shows that overestimation caused by function approximation, already recognized in value-based reinforcement learning, also affects actor-critic methods. The problem therefore concerns both the accuracy of the critic and the decisions learned by the actor.

The proposed algorithm builds on Double Q-learning and uses the smaller estimate from two critics to limit overestimation. It also connects target networks with overestimation bias and proposes updating the policy less frequently. Delaying those updates is intended to reduce the error introduced at each policy update, complementing the more conservative use of critic estimates.

On the OpenAI Gym environments evaluated, the method outperforms the reported state of the art in every tested environment. These findings support addressing approximation error as a practical route to better actor-critic learning, with the empirical claim applying to the environments included in the evaluation.
icml-2018-addressing-function-approximat.tldr: Using the smaller of two critic estimates and delaying policy updates reduces the effects of approximation error in actor-critic learning.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms generate a sequence of successive estimates, but their behavior can also be studied through a continuous mathematical model. This paper develops that connection for the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, and an accelerated variant. Its aim is to understand these algorithms using tools for systems that evolve continuously over time.

The authors derive differential equations describing the continuous limits of the algorithms' iterates. These equations provide another way to examine how the optimization process moves and how it behaves near critical points. Including both ordinary and accelerated ADMM brings both update schemes into the same broad style of analysis.

The paper then uses the direct method of Lyapunov to analyze stability and derive associated convergence rates. Stability concerns the behavior of trajectories near critical points, while convergence rates describe how quickly the modeled process approaches its limiting behavior. The contribution is an analytical connection between ADMM and dynamical systems, with results established through the continuous models.
icml-2018-admm-and-accelerated-admm-as-c.tldr: Continuous-time models of ADMM and accelerated ADMM enable Lyapunov-based analysis of stability and convergence rates.

paragraphs: Training a reinforcement learning agent around one reward-defined task does not directly provide a way to learn a diverse collection of tasks. This paper tackles the problem of discovering what an agent can accomplish in its environment. Its motivating examples include reaching different positions and moving objects to different locations.

A generator network proposes goals for the agent, with each goal expressed as reaching a parameterized subset of possible states. Adversarial training adjusts the generator to produce tasks at a suitable difficulty for the agent. The resulting sequence of goals acts as an automatically produced curriculum, linking task selection to the agent's developing capabilities.

The authors show that this framework can efficiently learn a broad set of tasks without prior knowledge of the environment, including settings with sparse rewards. The significance is that choosing learning goals becomes part of the learning process itself. The method supplies both tasks to attempt and a mechanism for keeping those tasks aligned with the agent's progress.
icml-2018-automatic-goal-generation-for-.tldr: An adversarially trained goal generator creates an adaptive curriculum that helps reinforcement learning agents discover and learn many tasks.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning both involve choices that influence another learning process. This paper places them in a common bilevel framework: an inner objective describes one optimization problem, while outer variables govern choices around it. Depending on the application, those outer variables represent supervised-learning hyperparameters or parameters of a meta-learner.

The approach solves an approximate bilevel problem by explicitly accounting for the optimization dynamics of the inner objective. The authors provide sufficient conditions under which solutions of this approximation converge to solutions of the exact problem. This gives a conditional theoretical justification for using the approximation, rather than asserting that every approximate formulation will recover an exact solution.

For deep meta-learning, the paper treats representation layers as hyperparameters shared across training episodes. Experiments support the theoretical findings, report encouraging few-shot learning results, and compare the approach with classical learning-to-learn methods. Together, these contributions connect a general optimization formulation with a concrete way to learn representations shared across episodes.
icml-2018-bilevel-programming-for-hyperp.tldr: A bilevel optimization framework unifies hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning, with sufficient conditions for convergence of approximate solutions.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using information from a teacher model. It is commonly used to transfer performance into a smaller student. This paper examines a different use: the student has the same parameterization as its teacher, so the central question is whether the transfer procedure can improve performance without changing model capacity.

The resulting Born-Again Networks significantly outperform their teachers in the reported computer vision and language modeling experiments. DenseNet-based experiments achieve reported state-of-the-art validation errors of 3.5% on CIFAR-10 and 15.5% on CIFAR-100. These results show that, in the evaluated settings, distillation can serve as a way to improve a model even when compression is not the objective.

The authors also investigate Confidence-Weighted by Teacher Max and Dark Knowledge with Permuted Predictions as alternative distillation objectives. These experiments examine how teacher outputs influence learning through both predicted and non-predicted classes. They help clarify which aspects of the teacher's output contribute to the benefits observed during knowledge transfer.
icml-2018-born-again-neural-networks-5ce.tldr: Students with the same parameterization as their teachers can outperform them through knowledge distillation.

paragraphs: Many continuous control problems allow actions only within specified bounds. A policy may nevertheless generate an action outside those bounds, requiring it to be clipped before execution. The paper identifies a mismatch in the usual learning procedure: policy optimization commonly treats the sampled action as though this clipping had not occurred.

Clipped Action Policy Gradient, or CAPG, incorporates knowledge of clipping into the gradient estimator. The purpose is to reduce variability in the estimated learning signal by accounting for how actions are actually executed. The authors prove that the estimator is unbiased and has lower variance than the conventional estimator that ignores the action bounds.

Experiments show that CAPG generally performs better than the conventional estimator. The theoretical result establishes properties of gradient estimation, while the empirical result supports its usefulness for learning control policies. The broader contribution is a way to use an existing feature of bounded-action environments to improve estimation, with experimental superiority described as general rather than universal.
icml-2018-clipped-action-policy-gradient.tldr: CAPG accounts for action clipping to produce unbiased policy gradients with lower variance than an estimator that ignores action bounds.

paragraphs: The Gamma-Poisson model represents count data through probabilistic matrix factorization. Its components include a topic or dictionary matrix and a score or activation matrix. This paper develops a reformulation that removes the activation matrix from the model expression through marginalization, allowing the dictionary to be studied through a marginal likelihood.

That reformulation provides insight into maximum marginal likelihood estimation of the dictionary. In particular, it explains why this estimator can remain robust when the chosen factorization rank is larger than needed. The authors connect this robustness to its ability to automatically prune irrelevant dictionary columns, a behavior previously observed empirically.

Marginalizing the activation matrix also leads to a new Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization algorithm with favorable properties. The contribution therefore combines an explanation of existing empirical behavior with a new estimation procedure. It shows how changing the mathematical representation of the model can clarify why unnecessary components disappear while also supporting a different approach to fitting the remaining dictionary.
icml-2018-closed-form-marginal-likelihoo.tldr: Marginalizing Gamma-Poisson activations explains dictionary pruning under excessive rank and yields a new Monte Carlo EM algorithm.

paragraphs: Neural networks are strong function approximators, but they are typically trained anew for each function. Gaussian Processes offer a different advantage: prior knowledge can support inference about a new function from limited observations. Their computational expense and the difficulty of selecting suitable priors motivate the paper's attempt to combine strengths of both approaches.

Conditional Neural Processes are neural models inspired by the flexibility of stochastic processes. They retain a neural-network structure and are trained using gradient descent. The intended capability is to make predictions about a function after seeing only a small collection of observations, while retaining the ability to handle complex functions and large datasets.

The authors report accurate predictions from only a handful of observed data points and demonstrate the approach on regression, classification, and image completion. These tasks illustrate the model family's versatility. The contribution is a shared modeling approach that connects learning from sparse observations with the scalability associated with neural networks across several kinds of prediction problems.
icml-2018-conditional-neural-processes-2.tldr: Conditional Neural Processes combine neural-network scalability with prediction about new functions from a small number of observations.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution by solving an optimization problem. This makes inference accessible to optimization methods, but the resulting objective is highly nonconvex for many models. Finding a good solution can therefore be difficult even after the original inference problem has been reformulated.

CRVI approaches this difficulty through convex relaxation and semidefinite programming. A relaxation provides a more tractable optimization formulation whose relationship to the original problem can be analyzed. The paper's theoretical results guarantee tight relaxation bounds that come closer to the global optimum than traditional coordinate ascent. The strength of this claim concerns the quality of the relaxation bounds, rather than an assertion that all original nonconvex problems are solved exactly.

The authors evaluate the approach on regression and sparse coding. These applications connect the theoretical construction to concrete inference problems. The main contribution is a way to address nonconvexity in variational optimization while obtaining guarantees about proximity to the global optimum through the relaxation.
icml-2018-crvi-convex-relaxation-for-var.tldr: CRVI uses convex relaxation and semidefinite programming to obtain tight bounds for nonconvex variational inference problems.

paragraphs: Learning systems with stochastic computation graphs often use score-function estimators to compute gradients. A surrogate loss makes first-order gradient estimation relatively straightforward, but extending that construction to higher derivatives creates difficulties. The paper shows that treating part of a cost as a fixed sample can produce missing or incorrect terms when further derivatives are taken.

DiCE replaces repeated, order-specific surrogate constructions with one objective that can be differentiated repeatedly. Each differentiation generates a correct estimator for the corresponding derivative order. Automatic differentiation performs the required graph manipulations, avoiding the increasingly cumbersome manual constructions associated with applying the surrogate-loss approach separately at successive orders.

The authors establish correctness through a proof and numerical evaluation of derivative estimates. They also use DiCE to develop and evaluate a new approach to multi-agent learning. The contribution matters when learning depends on derivatives beyond the first order: it provides a consistent objective whose repeated differentiation preserves the required stochastic terms instead of silently dropping them.
icml-2018-dice-the-infinitely-differenti.tldr: DiCE provides a single automatically differentiable objective that generates correct stochastic derivative estimators at any order.

paragraphs: SCAL addresses exploration and exploitation in unknown, weakly communicating Markov Decision Processes. Its key requirement is a known upper bound c on the span of the optimal bias function. This quantity offers an alternative to the MDP diameter, which can be much larger and can even be infinite in noncommunicating cases.

For S states, A actions, and at most Γ possible next states, the authors prove regret of order c√(ΓSAT). The significance is the dependence on the bias-span bound rather than a linear dependence on diameter, as in the cited existing algorithms. This can yield a substantially better guarantee when the span is small relative to the diameter.

A similar theoretical result existed for REGAL.C without a tractable algorithm. The paper relaxes its central optimization problem and supplies a computationally efficient solution. Simulations support the analysis and show SCAL significantly outperforming UCRL in large-diameter, small-span environments, connecting the favorable theoretical dependence to observed performance in that setting.
icml-2018-efficient-bias-span-constraine.tldr: SCAL efficiently explores unknown weakly communicating MDPs using a known bias-span bound, improving guarantees when diameter is large relative to span.

paragraphs: Expected policy gradients involve integrals that can be difficult to evaluate across different policy and critic choices. This paper develops a Fourier-analysis approach to deriving those updates. It rewrites the relevant integrals as convolutions and then turns the convolutions into multiplications, providing a route to analytical solutions.

The resulting solutions extend the low-variance benefits of expected policy gradients to a broad range of settings. The analysis covers trigonometric and radial basis critics, two families with universal approximation properties. Policy choices can be almost arbitrary, including mixtures and distributions that combine continuous and discrete components, making the framework applicable beyond a narrow pairing of policy and critic.

The paper also derives a general family of sample-based stochastic policy-gradient estimators that unifies existing approximation results. Its contribution joins analytical integration and sampling within one mathematical approach. The authors suggest that this could influence future policy-gradient methods; that prospective impact is presented as a possibility, while the analytical derivations are the established contribution.
icml-2018-fourier-policy-gradients-83893.tldr: Fourier analysis yields analytical expected policy gradients for broad policy and critic families and unifies sample-based estimators.

paragraphs: Predictive environment models can support reinforcement learning through representation learning or explicit planning. Building such models becomes difficult in larger environments, especially when observations reveal only part of the world or the environment is three-dimensional. This paper introduces an action-conditioned generative model designed for those more demanding settings.

The architecture combines a nonparametric spatial memory with learned, disentangled representations of the environment. A state-space model computes low-dimensional spatial updates using prior knowledge about the moving agent's dynamics. A Variational Auto-Encoder handles high-dimensional visual observations, giving spatial updating and visual modeling distinct roles within the overall predictive system.

The resulting architecture produces coherent predictions over hundreds of time steps across a range of partially observed 2D and 3D environments. This finding supports the proposed combination of memory, motion modeling, and visual generation as a scalable approach to temporal prediction. The reported result concerns the quality and duration of environment predictions, the capability needed before such models can support downstream planning or learning.
icml-2018-generative-temporal-models-wit.tldr: A generative model combining spatial memory, motion dynamics, and visual modeling makes coherent long-horizon predictions in partially observed environments.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods directly optimize a policy's performance and can operate without explicit knowledge of the underlying system. These features make them appealing for continuous control. However, even the linear quadratic regulator leads to a nonconvex optimization problem when approached through policy gradients, raising questions about whether optimization can reliably find the best policy.

This paper establishes global convergence to the optimal solution for model-free policy-gradient methods in the linear quadratic regulator setting. It also shows that the methods have polynomial sample and computational complexity in relevant problem-dependent quantities. The analysis therefore addresses both the quality of the eventual solution and the resources needed to obtain it.

The result gives direct policy optimization a firmer theoretical basis in this control problem, helping close a gap with system identification and model-based planning. Its significance is that nonconvexity does not prevent the analyzed methods from reaching the optimum efficiently in this setting. The stated guarantee concerns the linear quadratic regulator rather than arbitrary reinforcement learning problems.
icml-2018-global-convergence-of-policy-g.tldr: Model-free policy-gradient methods can solve the linear quadratic regulator globally with polynomial sample and computational complexity.

paragraphs: Embedding a hierarchy requires preserving the direction and organization of its relationships in a compact representation. This paper introduces a method for embedding directed acyclic graphs. It uses hyperbolic geometry, drawing on its proven advantages over Euclidean geometry for representing tree-like structures.

The central idea is to express hierarchical relationships as partial orders using nested, geodesically convex cones. These entailment cones give geometric form to the ordering relationships the embedding should preserve. The authors prove that the cones have an optimal shape with a closed-form expression in both Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces, and use this construction to define the embedding learning process.

Experiments show significant gains over strong recent baselines in representational capacity and generalization. The findings support combining a geometry suited to hierarchical structure with an explicit geometric representation of order. The contribution includes both a mathematical characterization of the cones and empirical evidence that the resulting embeddings better represent and generalize hierarchical relationships in the evaluated settings.
icml-2018-hyperbolic-entailment-cones-fo.tldr: Geometric entailment cones encode hierarchical order and improve the capacity and generalization of graph embeddings in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Models with hidden layers can discover abstract features automatically, but training them typically involves nonconvex optimization. Semidefinite programming relaxations offer a route toward global solutions. The paper identifies a drawback of existing approaches: their nonparametric, layer-wise kernel representations restrict them to transductive learning and slow prediction at test time.

The authors develop an inductive framework using parametric transfer functions and matching losses. Its purpose is to retain an optimization-based treatment of latent prediction while enabling a learned model to handle new inputs through a parametric representation. For ReLU transfer functions, the mathematical construction uses completely positive matrices.

The resulting inductive learner is reported to achieve superior accuracy and an order-of-magnitude speedup over SDP, together with constant approximation guarantees. These findings address both prediction quality and computational cost. The paper's contribution is therefore a framework for moving from the transductive formulation toward inductive prediction while preserving a stated form of approximation guarantee and improving reported practical performance.
icml-2018-inductive-two-layer-modeling-w.tldr: An inductive framework for parametric transfer functions improves reported accuracy and speed over SDP while providing constant approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Statistical testing on sensitive data must account for how information is collected as well as how it is analyzed. This paper studies hypothesis testing under local differential privacy, where participants' data are perturbed before sharing. The setup does not rely on a trusted collector being allowed to inspect every person's original record.

The authors focus on locally private chi-square tests for goodness of fit and independence. Goodness-of-fit testing asks whether data agree with a proposed distribution, while independence testing asks whether variables are statistically independent. Both questions must be addressed using entries that have already been altered to protect the participants who supplied them.

The contribution is an analysis of these testing problems within the local privacy model. This connects familiar statistical questions with a collection process that builds privacy into each participant's shared data. The distinction matters because the information available to the test is the perturbed data, making the privacy mechanism part of the statistical problem from the outset.
icml-2018-local-private-hypothesis-testi.tldr: The paper analyzes chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence tests when each participant's data are perturbed for local differential privacy.

paragraphs: Understanding a predictive problem often requires estimating how much different groups of features contribute to explaining an outcome. This paper treats that importance as a property of the underlying data-generating mechanism. The target is therefore broader than describing how one particular fitted prediction algorithm happens to use its inputs.

The proposed method connects this nonparametric view of importance with neural-network prediction. A single augmented network uses multi-task learning to estimate the importance of many feature subsets simultaneously. Bringing these estimates into one learning procedure improves on previous procedures for estimating importance and addresses the computational demands of examining multiple subsets.

On simulated data, the authors demonstrate both accuracy and computational efficiency. They also apply the method to a heart disease study and to mortality prediction for ICU patients. These results show how the estimation procedure can accompany practical predictive modeling. The contribution is an efficient way to estimate multiple feature-group contributions while maintaining a target defined by the underlying data distribution.
icml-2018-nonparametric-variable-importa.tldr: One augmented neural network uses multi-task learning to efficiently estimate the importance of many feature subsets.

paragraphs: Bayesian network structure learning can build a graph by learning local subgraphs and combining their information. This paper extends that approach to multiple agents working simultaneously. Each agent learns local subgraphs, creating opportunities for parallel work as well as for sharing information about overlapping learning problems.

The key improvement is that communication can reduce how much structure learning is needed in the first place. Agents store results from earlier queries and exchange even partial results. New inference rules relating query subsets and supersets allow many subgraph structures to be determined from this shared information without learning each one separately.

The authors provide a sound and complete parallel structure learning algorithm and demonstrate improved efficiency over state-of-the-art single-threaded algorithms. The result highlights two sources of efficiency: simultaneous work and the avoidance of redundant learning. The contribution is therefore more than distributing the original workload across agents; it uses the relationships between their queries to reduce that workload.
icml-2018-parallel-bayesian-network-stru.tldr: Parallel Bayesian network learners share query results to infer local structures and reduce redundant learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies two ways to complete a matrix with missing entries: minimize its rank or minimize its number of distinct rows. Both objectives seek a completed matrix with a form of simplicity. The analysis asks how computational difficulty depends on the organization of the missing entries.

The parameters include the smallest number of rows, columns, or rows and columns together needed to cover all missing positions. For bounded entry domains, both completion problems are fixed-parameter tractable with respect to each of these parameters. This means the algorithms can separate the difficult dependence on the selected parameter from polynomial dependence on the overall input size.

The authors also establish a lower bound for unbounded domains that rules out fixed-parameter tractability for some of the parameters studied. The domain restriction therefore matters to the computational picture. Together, the positive and negative results identify settings where a structured pattern of missing entries supports tractable parameterized algorithms and settings where that conclusion does not extend.
icml-2018-parameterized-algorithms-for-t.tldr: Two matrix completion objectives are fixed-parameter tractable for bounded domains under several parameters describing missing-entry locations.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms need to make effective decisions while learning from limited feedback. This paper seeks methods that combine practical usefulness with theoretical support. It brings together the empirical and computational advantages associated with realizability-based approaches and the flexibility associated with agnostic approaches.

The algorithms use a regression oracle for a class of value functions. This is presented as a more realistic computational building block than the classification oracles over policies commonly assumed by agnostic methods. The approach extends UCB and LinUCB to substantially more expressive model classes, allowing those familiar approaches to work within a broader modeling framework.

The authors establish low regret under certain distributional assumptions and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation. Their approach typically matches or exceeds the performance of both realizability-based and agnostic baselines. The theory is conditional on the stated kind of distributional assumptions, while the experiments support practical competitiveness rather than uniform superiority. Together, these results motivate regression as a useful foundation for general-purpose contextual bandit learning.
icml-2018-practical-contextual-bandits-w.tldr: Regression-oracle contextual bandits support expressive models, conditional low-regret guarantees, and competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Training a neural network across CPUs and GPUs requires deciding which device should execute each operation. Because the devices have different capabilities, these placement decisions affect total training time. Spotlight addresses the search for placements that make training faster, building on reinforcement learning approaches to this scheduling problem.

The method uses proximal policy optimization and models device placement as a multistage Markov decision process. This formulation is designed specifically for assigning neural-network operations to devices. It also enables a theoretical guarantee on performance improvements, connecting the learning algorithm with an analysis of the placement problem.

The authors implement Spotlight on the CIFAR-10 benchmark and deploy it on Google Cloud. In their experiments, training with Spotlight's recommended placements takes 60.9% of the time required by placements recommended by the policy-gradient comparison method. This result demonstrates a substantial reduction in measured training time in the evaluated setup; the theoretical improvement guarantee is not presented as a claim that every placement found is globally optimal.
icml-2018-spotlight-optimizing-device-pl.tldr: Spotlight uses proximal policy optimization for device placement, reducing measured training time to 60.9% of its policy-gradient comparator.

paragraphs: Structured predictions contain multiple related labels, and a model may benefit from leaving some labels unanswered. This paper introduces Structured Output Learning with Abstention, or SOLA, to make that choice part of prediction. Users can flexibly specify the cost of abstaining, allowing the prediction objective to reflect how unanswered labels should be treated.

The framework learns two predictors: one for structured abstention and another for structured outputs. Asymmetric, abstention-aware losses compare fully labeled training examples with predictions that may omit some labels. Learning uses surrogate regression in a feature space, and a new pre-image problem converts the result into a structured prediction with abstentions.

SOLA provides statistical guarantees on excess risk and is instantiated with a hierarchical abstention-aware loss for fine-grained opinion mining. The authors report state-of-the-art results on that task. They also show that the representations support competitive user-review rating prediction using a sentence-level opinion predictor. The work connects selective structured prediction with both theoretical support and practical opinion-analysis applications.
icml-2018-structured-output-learning-wit.tldr: SOLA learns structured predictions with selective abstention, user-defined abstention costs, and statistical excess-risk guarantees.

paragraphs: Graphics engines can express images through high-level programs, providing structure that a generic image decoder may lack. This paper uses that idea to address image interpretation and generation. It targets difficulties in previous renderer-based approaches, including hand-designed comparison functions, extensive supervision, and inference procedures that struggle with richer datasets.

SPIRAL trains an agent to produce programs that a graphics engine executes. A discriminator learns to distinguish real images from rendered ones, and the agent learns through distributed reinforcement learning to fool that discriminator. The system is trained without supervision, using the adversarial signal to guide the generation of image-producing programs.

The authors identify the discriminator's output as the key reward signal enabling meaningful progress toward matching the desired rendering. They demonstrate the approach on MNIST, Omniglot, CelebA, and synthetic 3D data. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first end-to-end unsupervised adversarial inverse-graphics demonstration on such challenging datasets. The findings support learned visual feedback as a way to train program-generating image agents.
icml-2018-synthesizing-programs-for-imag.tldr: SPIRAL uses adversarial rewards and reinforcement learning to generate graphics programs without supervision.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning represents a data point as a linear combination of learned dictionary columns. This paper studies how many training samples are needed for such representations to generalize, using dictionaries whose columns have unit norm. Coefficients are selected through a reconstruction objective that also imposes a constraint or encourages sparsity.

The analysis covers a family of reconstruction losses formed by minimizing a squared-distance term plus a radial penalty defined through an even univariate function. The authors connect this construction to Moreau envelopes. This gives a mathematical basis for studying dictionary learning with the specified loss family rather than only one reconstruction loss.

For the k-sparse dictionary problem, a new sample-complexity result removes a coherence condition imposed in earlier work. The derived generalization bounds scale as O(√(log n / n)) and require no additional restrictions on the class of dictionaries with unit-norm columns. The paper also discusses approximation error for certain loss families, connecting the choice of reconstruction loss with the theoretical analysis of learning.
icml-2018-the-generalization-error-of-di.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for a family of dictionary-learning losses and removes a previous coherence restriction for sparse dictionaries.
